brief: I want a small 3x3 USB macro keypad for my desk: nine mechanical keys I can map to shortcuts, plugs into my laptop over USB, no drivers.
summary: Raspberry Pi Pico soldered flat to a 2-layer PCB with 9 Kailh hot-swap sockets for MX switches, directly wired to 9 GPIOs. Two-part 3D printed case: the top doubles as the switch plate, the bottom tray holds the PCB on standoffs. Four M3 screws into heat-set inserts.
architecture: USB micro-B on the Pico -> VBUS 5V -> Pico VSYS (no external regulator)
9 switches, one per GPIO (GP2-GP10) to GND, internal pull-ups, no diodes or matrix
Firmware: KMK on CircuitPython, keymap in code.py
Stack (top down): keycaps, switches clipped into 1.5 mm printed plate, PCB 5.0 mm below plate top, sockets under PCB, tray
assembly: Order the PCB (Gerbers in pcb/) and the two case prints (fab/top.stl and fab/bottom.stl, PETG, 0.2 mm layers, top printed plate-down).
Solder the 9 hot-swap sockets onto the back of the PCB while it is bare and lies flat, face down.
Turn it face up (it rests level on its sockets) and solder the Pico flat onto the PCB by its castellated edges, USB end flush with the right edge.
Flash the Pico: hold BOOTSEL, plug it in, copy CircuitPython onto the RPI-RP2 drive, then KMK onto CIRCUITPY. Unplug. (Later, the small hole in the lid reaches BOOTSEL.)
Press the 4 M3 heat-set inserts into the top shell's bosses with a soldering iron at about 220 °C, then set the top on the PCB.
Clip the 9 switches into the plate, pressing each until its two pins seat in its socket; keep the PCB flat on the bench so the sockets are backed.
Set it all in the tray and fasten with the 4 M3 screws from below.
Press a keycap onto each switch.

Plug the USB cable into the Pico and copy code.py onto CIRCUITPY with GP2-GP10 mapped to your shortcuts. Keys are numbered from the bottom left, row by row (K1 to K3 along the bottom, K7 to K9 along the top, the USB end on the right), and the board wires K1 GP10, K2 GP7, K3 GP4, K4 GP9, K5 GP6, K6 GP3, K7 GP8, K8 GP5, K9 GP2; the labels under the keys say the same.
Test: each key should send its shortcut. If one doesn't, check its socket joint first.

designMd:
# Macro keypad: design (stage 1)

**Request:** a 3×3 USB macro keypad, nine mechanical keys, no drivers. One unit, US, $75 budget.

**Concept:** the simplest proven build. A Raspberry Pi Pico is soldered flat onto a small 2-layer PCB. Each of the nine
switches goes to its own GPIO and to ground, so there is no matrix and no diodes. Switches sit in hot-swap sockets, so
no switch is ever soldered. A two-part printed case: the top is also the switch plate.

**Architecture:** see `design.json` → `architecture`. All dimensions live in `design.json` → `params`; the CAD
(`cad/*.py` in this folder) and the engineer checks (design stage) both read them from there, so they can't drift apart.

**Stack, top down:** keycaps → switches clipped into the 1.5 mm plate → PCB top 5.0 mm below the plate top
(the MX standard) → hot-swap sockets under the PCB → 4 mm standoffs → 2 mm tray floor → rubber feet.

**Layout (PCB 61 × 94 mm):** keys on a 19.05 mm grid starting 5.4 mm from the near edge; the Pico across the top, USB
end flush with the right edge so the cable reaches it; M3 holes 3.5 mm in from each corner, kept 4 mm clear of the
Pico. The 8.4 mm insert bosses run from the PCB up to the plate beside the corner switches, so each hole centre stays
4.4 mm (boss radius plus 0.2 mm) from every switch housing; the check `holes-clear-keys` measures it. The case is
66.8 × 99.8 mm, just under the 100 mm the request allows.

**Lid over the Pico:** a 3 mm hole over the BOOTSEL button (a paperclip reflashes it without opening the case) and a
1.6 mm window over the LED. Their positions are estimates (see `design.json` → `estimates`): check them against your
Pico before printing the top.

**Changed:** the first layout had the PCB 90 mm tall with the keys 1.9 mm from its edge, which put the two near bosses
1.3 mm from the corner switches' housings, so those switches could not clip in. The board grew 4 mm and the grid
moved up 3.5 mm. The feet are Adafruit 550's real size, 8 mm across and 4 mm tall (they were 10 × 3).

**Firmware:** KMK on CircuitPython. Each key maps to a shortcut in `code.py`; the Pico shows up as a USB keyboard.
The keys are wired to the GPIOs in the order the Pico's pads allow, not in key order (the tracks on the back cannot
cross): K1 is the bottom left key, K3 bottom right, K7 top left, K9 top right, and the board wires K1 GP10, K2 GP7,
K3 GP4, K4 GP9, K5 GP6, K6 GP3, K7 GP8, K8 GP5, K9 GP2. `cad/pcb.mjs` returns this map and warns if `design.json`'s
assembly stops giving it.

**Parts, grouped (Anatomy-style):**
- Base: tray, 4 standoffs, 4 rubber feet, 4 button-head screws
- Structure: top shell and plate, 4 insert bosses, 4 heat-set inserts, PCB
- Mechanism: 9 switches, 9 hot-swap sockets
- Controls: 9 keycaps
- Subject: the Pico and its USB port

**Figure:** `figure.mjs` draws this stack in the Anatomy style from the same `params` and the BOM specs: every part at
its real count, an apart pose that lifts each layer off along its way in, and nine assembly steps in build order
(`distinta figure macropad`, then open `view.html`). The parts the case hides (the PCB, the Pico, the sockets, the
inserts, the screws and the feet) show as dashed outlines while they are lit and something covers them.

# Build plan: 3x3 USB macro keypad

> I want a small 3x3 USB macro keypad for my desk: nine mechanical keys I can map to shortcuts, plugs into my laptop over USB, no drivers.

**1 unit · $92.29 for parts, fab and estimated shipping · longest lead 12 days**
Budget $75.00: OVER budget.

## What it is
Raspberry Pi Pico soldered flat to a 2-layer PCB with 9 Kailh hot-swap sockets for MX switches, directly wired to 9 GPIOs. Two-part 3D printed case: the top doubles as the switch plate, the bottom tray holds the PCB on standoffs. Four M3 screws into heat-set inserts.

## Assembly
1. Order the PCB (Gerbers in pcb/) and the two case prints (fab/top.stl and fab/bottom.stl, PETG, 0.2 mm layers, top printed plate-down).
2. Solder the 9 hot-swap sockets onto the back of the PCB while it is bare and lies flat, face down.
3. Turn it face up (it rests level on its sockets) and solder the Pico flat onto the PCB by its castellated edges, USB end flush with the right edge.
4. Flash the Pico: hold BOOTSEL, plug it in, copy CircuitPython onto the RPI-RP2 drive, then KMK onto CIRCUITPY. Unplug. (Later, the small hole in the lid reaches BOOTSEL.)
5. Press the 4 M3 heat-set inserts into the top shell's bosses with a soldering iron at about 220 °C, then set the top on the PCB.
6. Clip the 9 switches into the plate, pressing each until its two pins seat in its socket; keep the PCB flat on the bench so the sockets are backed.
7. Set it all in the tray and fasten with the 4 M3 screws from below.
8. Stick on the 4 rubber feet.
9. Press a keycap onto each switch.
10. Plug the USB cable into the Pico and copy code.py onto CIRCUITPY with GP2-GP10 mapped to your shortcuts. Keys are numbered from the bottom left, row by row (K1 to K3 along the bottom, K7 to K9 along the top, the USB end on the right), and the board wires K1 GP10, K2 GP7, K3 GP4, K4 GP9, K5 GP6, K6 GP3, K7 GP8, K8 GP5, K9 GP2; the labels under the keys say the same.
11. Test: each key should send its shortcut. If one doesn't, check its socket joint first.

### What goes on at each step (from the figure)
Open `view.html` and walk the steps with ← → (or choose one under Build), or open `view.html#step=<n>` for one.

| Step | Do | Parts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Start with the bare PCB | 1 × Keypad PCB |
| 2 | Solder the 9 sockets onto the back | 9 × Kailh MX hot-swap socket |
| 3 | Solder the Pico flat onto the face | 1 × Raspberry Pi Pico |
| 4 | Press the 4 inserts in, set the top on | 4 × M3 heat-set insert, 1 × Case top / switch plate |
| 5 | Clip the 9 switches into the plate | 9 × MX-compatible mechanical switch |
| 6 | Set it in the tray, 4 screws from below | 4 × M3 x 8 button head screw, 1 × Case bottom tray |
| 7 | Stick on the 4 rubber feet | 4 × Adhesive rubber foot |
| 8 | Press a keycap onto each switch | 9 × 1u keycap, MX stem |
| 9 | Plug the USB cable into the Pico | 1 × USB micro-B cable, 1 m |

In production/ these sit next to this plan; in the product folder they are at the paths shown.
